eligibility_reason: Skills are stored as versioned SKILL.md artifacts (YAML metadata + markdown body) that the system writes to at run time and later reads to condition agent behaviour on new tasks (p. 3: 'Each skill is a self-contained SKILL.md artifact... a versionable, retrievable unit of procedural memory'; p. 10: 'Each skill is stored as a versioned textual artifact... a SKILL.md file'). The write is explicit: an update operator maps a trace pool collected from execution to a new skill version, s(v+1) = U(s(v), Dsrc) (p. 4), driven by a 'reflector' that inspects traces and proposes a revised body (p. 4), executed through a COLLECT-DIAGNOSE-REVISE-PROMOTE cycle (p. 10). The evolved skill is then used to condition the agent on later tasks, roles and model backbones (p. 2, p. 4 Sec. 4), i.e. cross-session state that shapes future behaviour, satisfying I1. Year is 2026 (I2), text is English full text with 19 extracted pages, well beyond abstract-only (I3, I4, E7 not triggered). Not a survey (E4 not triggered); memory is the paper's central contribution, not incidental (E5 not triggered); not hardware/parametric-only/fixed-corpus memory (E1-E3 not triggered).

facets.justification: Skills are versioned textual files: 'a SKILL.md file contains YAML metadata and a markdown body' (p. 10, Appendix B, Skill representation); also p. 3: 'Each skill is a self-contained SKILL.md artifact in the Agent Skills format... a versionable, retrievable unit'; p. 4: 'Skills are stored as versioned SKILL.md artifacts with YAML metadata and markdown bodies'. No vector, graph, or relational store is described in the given pages.

p. 4 defines 'the reflector: the model or procedure that inspects traces, summarizes failure modes, and proposes a revised skill body' -- new content synthesised from a trace pool, not present in any single source trace. p. 10 confirms the mechanism: 'the framework aggregates failure traces into recurrent error modes... A revision operator proposes a candidate body conditioned on the current skill and the diagnosis.' This is the transformation the paper evaluates (single-refinement results, p. 17).

The paper explicitly removes retrieval from the studied mechanism: 'Skill annotations are fixed at task definition rather than retrieved at solve time, separating skill quality from retrieval quality... retrieval can be studied as a separate problem on the same tasks' (p. 3). None of the given pages (1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 17, 18) describe how a skill re-enters context during deployment/use -- retrieval is deliberately held out of scope, so no value on the enumerated scale (including 'none_declared', which implies an undescribed-but-present mechanism) can be anchored to text I was given.

All reported results are on the authors' own constructed benchmark (AFTER, 382 tasks, 6 roles) under controlled splits for specificity and generality (p. 2, p. 4 Sec. 2.3-3), with accuracy-metric comparisons across model sizes in Table K.1 (p. 17). No real users, fielded deployment, or production setting outside the authors' own experimental protocol is reported in the given pages, despite the abstract's framing toward 'production agent platforms' (p. 1) -- per the guide, that framing without an outside-the-lab setting codes as validation, taken conservatively.

Systems are run over the fixed AFTER task suite and scored with M1/M2 accuracy metrics (p. 4, Eq. 1-2), reported per role/model in Table K.1 (p. 17: Hpre/Hpost columns per role, aggregate delta +3.7 to +6.7). No control-group manipulation beyond fixed benchmark splits, and no case study or simulation is described in the given pages.

The first contribution bullet on p. 2 names 'AFTER, a benchmark for procedural skill transfer in LLM agents' -- 382 tasks, 6 roles, 22 skills, with controlled transfer splits -- as the artefact offered to the reader; Table 1 (p. 2) compares it against prior benchmarks. The second bullet (empirical evidence via the EVOLUTION protocol) reports findings produced using AFTER rather than naming EVOLUTION itself as the primary deliverable.
